newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals -- Japan eyes talks on 1997 purchases.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals -- Japan eyes talks on 1997 purchases.

text.p: Japan's metal markets have turned their attention to coming talks on purchase contracts for 1997, traders said on Wednesday, after informal discussions began last week at the London Metal Exchange's Metals Week.

Copper traders also expected announcements on premiums in the next week or two from copper refiners in Zambia and the Philippines, after Codelco announced in late September that it would leave its premium for shipments to Japan next year unchanged at $50 per tonne over LME cash settlement prices.

In the zinc market, traders said forecasts for 1997 zinc supply and demand, released on Tuesday by the International Lead and Zinc Study Group (ILZSG), brought few surprises, suggesting some potential tightness in the Asia-Pacific region although supply availability should be sufficient on a global level.
The ILZSG estimated mine supplies next year would rise 3.9 percent to 7.33 million tonnes, while demand would increase 2.8 percent to 7.77 million tonnes.

Traders said they expected Japan's premiums for Chinese refined zinc to be set at around $80 to $90 a tonne in supply contracts for next year, although they had already detected purchases from China by Japanese smelters, who sell imported metal as well as their own output, at premiums of about $105.
Traders said, however, that Japan's smelters tend to offer generous premiums in an effort to discourage cheap imports that could undercut prices for their domestic output.
A Japanese smelter official countered that premiums on Chinese metal were expected to rise next year due to strong demand from booming Southeast Asian economies.
Japan's total refined zinc imports were expected to decline next year, due to overbuying this year in a rush to cover lost output after two Japanese zinc refiners were shut.
For zinc concentrates, market sources expected treatment charges to be largely unchanged from last year's $190 per tonne, based on an LME price of $1,000 per tonne.
The copper and zinc spot markets were deadly quiet this week, traders said, and they expected them to remain so through the end of the year.

Aluminium premiums were little changed in the past week, traders said, as end users waited for a bottoming out in LME prices after they slid more than $200 in little more than a month to a 2 1/2-year low of $1,305 a tonne last Thursday.
Benchmark three-month LME aluminium prices managed a bounce on Tuesday, closing $29 higher on the day at $1,356 a tonne.
Traders said intermerchant activity had picked up in Japan in recent days, although end users were still sidelined.
"They all think the LME downtrend will continue," said one Japanese trader. "I don't think (Tuesday's gains) were connected to actual demand."
Traders also said a continued slide in the yen against the dollar offset some of the fall in dollar-based aluminium prices.
One added, however, that an apparent pickup in premiums in the U.S. Midwest may spill over into Japan as well.
